task_description: The script calculates geometric properties (area, perimeter) of a given polygon geometry after reprojection to EPSG:3857, and raster-based statistics (elevation mean/min/max and slope mean) from a DSM layer within that polygon. Elevation statistics are computed using QgsZonalStatistics directly on the input DSM layer; slope statistics require QGIS Processing framework initialization and execution of the 'native:slope' algorithm, followed by zonal statistics on the derived slope layer. If processing is unavailable, slope calculation is skipped and slope_mean remains None.

task_name: Visualize solar energy and photovoltaic yield
task_description: The script visualizes 3D solar energy and photovoltaic (PV) yield models using DSM (digital surface model), roof/ground irradiance or PV yield rasters, wall energy text files, and vegetation data. It loads geospatial layers into QGIS, allows interactive area selection via bounding rectangle, clips raster data to the selected extent using GDAL, reads clipped DSM and energy arrays into NumPy, processes wall energy data via a threaded worker, and renders a 3D OpenGL visualization with interactive controls (rotation, zoom, shift) and a dynamic colorbar scaled to irradiance [kWh/m²] or PV yield [kWh/kWp]. Outputs include an interactive 3D scene, colorbar legend, and optional screenshot export.

The script performs regression-based unmixing to estimate sub-pixel class fractions (e.g., endmember abundances) from a raster layer using synthetically mixed training data derived from a classification dataset of spectral endmembers. It constructs an ensemble of regressors (one per run), each trained on a unique synthetic mixture set generated via PrepareRegressionDatasetFromSynthMixAlgorithm; predicts fraction maps per class per run; aggregates predictions across runs using either mean±std or median±IQR (configurable); enforces optional sum-to-one constraint via raster math; outputs three rasters: (1) class fraction layer (multi-band, one band per class), (2) optional classification layer derived from argmax of fractions, and (3) optional variation layer (std or IQR per class). No specific study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is referenced — inputs are generic raster layers and classification datasets (e.g., .pkl endmember libraries), with no embedded temporal or platform metadata. All geospatial operations (stacking, aggregation, normalization, translation) are applied post-prediction using GDAL and EnMAP-Box algorithms.

The script performs a pixel-wise summation of multiple input binary (0/1) raster layers to produce a single output raster where each pixel value equals the count of input rasters with value 1 at that location. It uses QGIS’s QgsRasterCalculator to evaluate the formula 'raster1@1 + raster2@1 + ...' over the common extent and resolution of the first input raster. No normalization, classification, or external geospatial data (e.g., satellite imagery, time series, or study area definitions) is present in the code — it is a generic, geometry-agnostic raster algebra operation. Input rasters must be pre-binarized; no band selection, sensor processing, temporal filtering, or spatial subsetting occurs. The output is a GeoTIFF raster file named 'Boolean Overlay Map'.

The script performs a spatial constraint checking task by interrogating user-defined spatial datasets (e.g., PostGIS, Spatialite, SQL Server) for features intersecting or within a buffer of a query geometry (point, line, or polygon). It reads configuration from config.cfg and XG_SYS.ini, applies WHERE clauses to filter layers, computes distances, optionally includes descriptive fields, dates, and summary statistics, writes results to memory layers (point/line/polygon), inserts records into a configured database table (or creates a temporary one), and exports text/CSV reports. Outputs include a QGIS memory vector layer per geometry type, a tabular result model, and formatted text/CSV reports.

The script generates hypsometric curves from a digital elevation model (DEM) named 'dem_terrain.tif'. It first loads the DEM in QGIS, extracts its spatial extent and CRS, creates a boundary polygon matching that extent as a shapefile ('boundary.shp'), then runs the QGIS 'hypsometriccurves' algorithm with a 100-meter elevation step and percentage-based histogram output. The result is saved in the working directory as histogram files prefixed with 'histogram_' — indicating elevation distribution analysis by area percentage.

task_name: Reclassify and smooth NLCD land cover
task_description: The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) raster data for Alaska, specifically the 2016 Tree Canopy and Land Cover layers. It performs a sequence of geospatial operations: (1) reprojecting the input NLCD Land Cover raster to EPSG:4326; (2) reclassifying land cover classes into simplified grass-dominated values using a pixel-wise arithmetic expression mapping 20 original NLCD classes (e.g., 21=Developed, Open Space → 26; 41=Deciduous Forest → 23) to new integer codes; (3) separately reclassifying urban classes (21,22,23,24) into urban-subtype codes (10,1,1,2); (4) applying GRASS r.neighbors (median filter, size=7) to denoise and remove road/clutter artifacts from the urban layer; (5) compositing the cleaned urban layer over the grass-only layer using conditional pixel replacement (urban pixels override grass where present); (6) upscaling (8× finer resolution) via GDAL Warp with resampling; (7) spatially smoothing the high-resolution composite using GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11); and (8) compressing and exporting as an 8-bit LZW-compressed GeoTIFF. The final output is a smoothed, high-resolution, urban-prioritized, grass-background land cover raster in WGS84, named 'NLCD_2016_Alaska_SaintPaul-Island_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff'. Input filenames and paths confirm the source is NLCD 2016, and the processing is explicitly scoped to Alaska, specifically Saint Paul Island and adjacent longitude bands (e.g., 'Alaska141-140_60').

The script imports an EnMAP Level 1C product by reading its XML metadata file, extracting wavelength, FWHM, gain, and offset values per band, and generating a GDAL VRT raster file. It opens the corresponding SPECTRAL_IMAGE file (derived from the XML filename), sets ENVI metadata for wavelength (in nanometers) and FWHM, assigns band descriptions with center wavelengths, applies per-band scale (gain) and offset corrections via GDAL Band.SetScale/SetOffset, and flushes caches. The output is a calibrated, spectrally annotated VRT raster layer ready for analysis in EnMAP-Box; no classification, modeling, or time-series analysis is performed — only data import and radiometric scaling.

The script converts vector layer geometries to a specified target geometry type (Centroids, Nodes, Linestrings, Multilinestrings, or Polygons) while preserving Z/M coordinates if present. It processes each input feature, applies the selected conversion logic (e.g., computing centroids, extracting nodes, deriving boundaries for polygons, closing linestrings to form polygons), and outputs new features with the target WKB type and original attributes. The algorithm is implemented as a QGIS Processing algorithm with enum-based user selection and robust handling of geometry types, coordinate dimensions, and error cases.

The script classifies soil texture using user-provided sand and clay raster layers (loaded from QGIS map canvas) and a user-selected triangular texture classification schema file (.dat). It reads sand and clay pixel values, maps each (sand, clay) coordinate pair into a USDA or similar soil texture triangle defined by polygonal rules in the schema, assigns a numeric texture class code (e.g., 'SAND', 'CLAY', 'LOAM'), and outputs: (1) a classified GeoTIFF raster with Byte data type and -9999 NoData; (2) an optional vectorized shapefile with attribute fields 'code' and 'label_txt' derived from the schema’s legend; and (3) a CSV file ('_ternaryPlot.csv') containing per-pixel CLAY,SAND,SILT triplets for ternary plotting. The script operates entirely on local raster files — no GEE server-side computation is performed; it is a QGIS desktop plugin with GDAL/Numpy-based local raster processing. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code — inputs are arbitrary local rasters selected by the user via QGIS layer list.

task_name: Generate synthetic DSM from DTM and surface features
task_description: The script generates a synthetic Digital Surface Model (DSM) at 10m resolution by fusing a base DTM (Digital Terrain Model), building height data (rasterized from a GeoPackage of LoD1 buildings), canopy height model (CHM) from ETH, and land use masking (e.g., excluding water and bare soil). It performs raster alignment, NoData handling, height capping (≤100 m), and conditional addition of surface objects to terrain, outputting a georeferenced GeoTIFF DSM with -9999.0 as NoData value.

The script computes an urban change summary table by processing urban and population raster layers across multiple time periods (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015). It splits the area of interest along meridians, aligns rasters to pixel grids using GDAL VRTs, clips them to WKT geometries, and calculates class-wise urban area (in hectares) and associated population (persons per hectare) for up to 9 urban classes. The output includes a GeoTIFF (or VRT) stack with urban and population bands per year, and an Excel summary table populated into a template with pre-defined sheet layout and cell offsets (rows 23 and 37), plus logo insertion.

The script generalizes polygon and multipolygon features in a QGIS vector layer using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm (via QgsGeometry.simplify()) with a user-specified tolerance in map units. It supports two output modes: (1) creating a new temporary or permanent memory-based layer containing simplified geometries while preserving original attributes, or (2) in-place editing of the source layer’s geometries. Vertex counts before/after simplification are computed and reported, and history is recorded for undo support via base64-encoded WKB geometry backups. The action respects feature selection, handles edit mode automatically, and includes rollback-on-error and auto-commit capabilities.

task_name: Calculate Green-Ampt and SCS infiltration parameters
task_description: The script computes infiltration-related parameters for grid cells in a FLO-2D hydrodynamic model. It supports three methods: (1) Green-Ampt, which calculates weighted average hydraulic conductivity (XKSAT), soil water retention parameter (PSIF), change in soil moisture content (DTHETA), initial abstraction (IA), imperviousness-adjusted conductivity (XKsatc), and relative imperviousness (RTIMP) by intersecting soil and land use polygon layers with the computational grid; (2) SCS single-layer, which assigns Curve Number (CN) based on polygon centroid containment; (3) SCS multi-layer, which computes composite CN from land-soil type, cover density, and impervious fraction using empirical equations per vegetation/soil class. Outputs are dictionaries mapping grid IDs to parameter sets (e.g., {'hydc': 0.042, 'dtheta': 0.18, 'abstrinf': 0.1, 'scsn': 72}), optionally written to a diagnostic CSV file (GA_Diagnostics.csv) with columns including GridNum, SoilXKSAT, VCAdjustment, DTHETA, IA, PSIF, etc. All operations rely on QGIS vector/raster geometry intersection, spatial indexing, area-weighted averaging, logarithmic averaging (for PSIF/DTHETA when log_area_average=True), and GDAL-based raster resampling (gdalwarp) and nodata filling (gdal_fillnodata).

The script performs multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to compute and normalize spatial suitability maps for school and business development. It transforms input rasters (population density, road distance, slope, land use/land cover, water distance) using domain-specific reclassifications and inversions (e.g., '1 - slope@1' for lower-slope preference), applies distinct weighted linear combinations (school: 20% population, 30% roads, 25% slope, 15% LULC, 10% water; business: 45% roads, 35% population, 10% LULC, 10% slope), and normalizes final outputs to [0,1] using min-max scaling. Outputs include two normalized suitability rasters (school_suitability.tif, business_suitability.tif) and a difference raster (school_business_diff.tif).

The script smooths a user-provided input DEM raster (e.g., '/path/to/input_DEM.tif') within polygon boundaries defined in QGIS by solving Laplace's equation via harmonic interpolation — either using a direct sparse linear system solver (scipy) or iterative Gauss-Seidel relaxation. It preserves original elevation values on the polygon boundary (Dirichlet boundary conditions) to ensure seamless, continuous transitions with surrounding terrain, eliminating artificial seams or elevation jumps. The output is a modified DEM raster written to 'output_path' (e.g., '/path/to/output_DEM.tif'), where only pixels strictly interior to each polygon feature are updated; all other pixels retain their original values. No remote sensing data ingestion, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived processing occurs — inputs are local GeoTIFF and QGIS vector layers only.

task_name: Calculate driving time to polling stations
task_description: The script calculates driving time (or distance) from voting stations to population centroids using a road network in QGIS via the QNEAT3 plugin framework. It constructs a network graph from a road layer ('OSSroad2450'), ties origin points ('votingStations2450') and destination points ('populationCentroidWithID2450') to the network, computes shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm with speed-aware cost strategy (strategy_option=1), accounts for entry/exit costs, and exports results—including origin_id, destination_id, entry_cost, network_cost, exit_cost, and total_cost—to a CSV file named 'drivingTime.csv'.

task_name: Download satellite imagery for coastal monitoring
task_description: The script downloads Landsat 5, 7, 8, 9 and Sentinel-2 Level-1C (and Tier 2 for Landsat) imagery covering a user-defined polygon between specified dates. It applies cloud filtering (>95% cloud cover removed), adjusts the ROI polygon to align with image pixel grids to avoid resampling, downloads multispectral, panchromatic (L7/L8/L9), SWIR (S2), and QA bands separately per resolution, resamples bands to common grids (e.g., resample Landsat 5 MS to 15m, S2 SWIR to 10m), merges bands into stacked GeoTIFFs, writes metadata (date, filename, EPSG, georeferencing accuracy, radiometric quality, tilename, dimensions) to .txt files, and saves a consolidated metadata dictionary as a .pkl file. Outputs are organized in mission-specific subfolders (e.g., L5/10m/, L7/pan/, S2/20m/) under a site-named directory. No classification, change detection, or shoreline extraction is performed — this is purely a data acquisition and preprocessing pipeline for downstream CoastSat analysis.

The script computes thermal mean radiant temperature (TMRT) differences between shaded and sunlit areas using DSM, CDSM, building rasters, and precomputed shadow and TMRT rasters across multiple timesteps. It derives spatial reference (lat/lon) from the DSM projection, rasterizes a selected planting area polygon, applies buffering to avoid edge effects, groups shadow regions by overlapping timesteps, clips input rasters around the selected area using tree shadow extent buffers, and calculates TMRT in shade versus sunlit conditions for tree planting analysis.

task_name: Test vector layer ring addition and vertex editing
task_description: The script is a QGIS unit test suite validating the correctness of QgsVectorLayerEditUtils methods—including addRing, addRingV2, moveVertex, moveVertexV2, splitParts, mergeFeatures, and field split policies—on in-memory vector layers. It constructs synthetic geometries (e.g., polygons at coordinates like (0 0, 5 0, ...), points at (0 0), multipolygons forming a 3×2 grid), applies editing operations, and asserts expected WKT geometry outputs and attribute behaviors. No real-world study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial inputs are used; all data is programmatically generated for functional testing.

The script generates georeferenced 2-meter proximity buffers around lineaments extracted from Bhuvan WMS service. It fetches PNG images of state-level lineament layers (e.g., 'AN_LN50K_0506') via WMS GetMap requests using bounding box coordinates from 'bhuvan_extent.csv', converts them to binary masks (white = no lineament → 0, non-white → 1), georeferences the masks using EPSG:4326 and upper-left/lower-right coordinates, computes Euclidean proximity rasters (MAXDIST=2, DISTUNITS=GEO), thresholds to create 2m binary buffer masks, and re-georeferences those as final 'proxigeo_mask.tif' outputs per Indian state. The study area is India’s states (e.g., Andaman & Nicobar, code 'AN'), with no temporal component — all data are static lineament vector layers published on Bhuvan (NRSC) at 1:50K scale. Outputs are per-state GeoTIFFs in 'proxigeo_masks/' folder, representing 2m spatial buffers around mapped lineaments.

The script loads and manipulates geospatial data in QGIS via PyQGIS: (1) loads a Seoul administrative boundary shapefile (admin_emd.shp) and a DEM raster (dem30.tif); (2) performs attribute and spatial queries (e.g., feature ID=5, bounding box intersection); (3) computes raster values at point locations; (4) creates memory layers (buffered polygon, circular point distribution); (5) adds/calculates fields (x/y coordinates, elevation from DEM); (6) applies geometry operations (buffering, centroid, transformation between EPSG:4326 and EPSG:5174); (7) exports memory layers to Shapefile and GeoJSON; (8) uses QgsSpatialIndex for fast spatial joins between admin_sgg and stores layers. All operations are local-file-based — no GEE server-side computation occurs. The study area is explicitly Seoul (South Korea), using Korean CRS (EPSG:5174), EUC-KR encoding, and Korean administrative nomenclature (EMD_NM). No satellite imagery, time-series analysis, or Earth Engine API calls are present — this is purely a QGIS desktop automation script.

The script imports PRISMA Level 1 hyperspectral and panchromatic data from HDF5 (.he5) files into QGIS/GDAL-compatible formats (GTiff for spectral cubes and error matrices; VRT for all other sub-datasets). It extracts and restructures VNIR and/or SWIR spectral cubes (with wavelength/FWHM metadata), PAN cube, geolocation fields (latitude/longitude), pixel error matrices, and thematic masks (cloud, land cover, sun glint). The workflow includes band selection based on non-zero central wavelengths, transposition to fix BIP interleave, spectral stacking, no-data masking, and paletted rendering for categorical masks. All outputs are georeferenced, metadata-enriched, and styled for visualization in QGIS. The study area, time range, and geographic extent are not specified in the code — they are determined solely by the input HE5 file, which follows the PRISMA naming convention (e.g., 'PRS_L1_STD_OFFL_20201107101404_20201107101408_0001.he5') but no parsing or validation of acquisition timestamps or footprints is performed in the script.

task_name: Compute weighted overlay of infrastructure layers
task_description: The script performs a raster-based weighted overlay analysis using two input rasters (bohLayer and bohLayer1), computing the normalized difference ratio (boh1@1 - boh@1) / (boh1@1 + boh@1) — effectively a normalized index analogous to NDVI — and outputs a single GeoTIFF raster ('OUTPUT.tif') representing the spatial contrast or compositional balance between the two input thematic layers, likely representing competing or complementary urban infrastructure or land suitability factors.

The script eliminates sliver (small or narrow) polygons from a vector polygon layer by merging them with adjacent polygons based on user-defined selection criteria and merge rules. It supports three merge modes: largest area, smallest area, or largest common boundary. The input is a QGIS vector layer (polygon type); selection can be made either by attribute filtering (with configurable comparison operators including ==, !=, >, <, begins with, contains) or by using an existing selection. After identifying candidate polygons to eliminate, the script iteratively attempts to merge each with a neighboring polygon satisfying intersection and geometric criteria (e.g., shared boundary length or area), updates the geometry in-place, and writes all remaining features—including unmerged slivers—to a new output vector layer. No raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, or external geospatial datasets are involved; it is purely a vector topological cleaning operation within QGIS Processing Framework. The script does not specify any study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, or external data sources—it operates solely on the provided local vector layer.

The script is a QGIS plugin testing module that generates synthetic and real-world spectral library test data for unit testing. It loads an embedded EnMAP hyperspectral raster ('enmap.tif') to extract core spectral data (reflectance cube), wavelength metadata, and georeferencing information. Using this, it creates randomized spectral profiles with configurable numbers of bands per profile field, supports coordinate transformations between source and target CRS, and builds fully functional QgsVectorLayer-based spectral libraries with proper profile fields, geometries, and encoded spectral values. Key outputs include in-memory GDAL datasets (e.g., '/vsimem/testImage.*.tif'), QgsRasterLayer and QgsVectorLayer instances (including from GeoJSON test data 'testvectordata.geojson'), and mocked QGIS application interfaces (QgsApplication, QgisInterface) for headless testing. No remote sensing analysis or classification is performed — the purpose is deterministic, reproducible test object generation for spectral library functionality.

The script loads a Dutch municipal boundaries WFS layer (gemeenten2014) in EPSG:28992, filters features to retain only those with non-null 'gemeentenaam' attribute, selects those features, exports the selection to a GeoJSON file, removes the original WFS layer from QGIS, and re-adds the exported GeoJSON as a new vector layer. The output is a cleaned GeoJSON file containing only municipalities with valid names.

The script places villa footprints in optimal locations using a greedy algorithm that sorts candidate locations by suitability score (0–100) from a raster input, enforces minimum edge-to-edge spacing between villas, and generates rectangular footprint polygons with configurable dimensions and rotation. It filters candidates to a buildable envelope polygon if provided, outputs a GeoPackage containing villa geometries and metadata (villa_id, score, rotation, dimensions, center coordinates), and reports statistics including count placed, total building area, and mean suitability score.

task_name: Download ETH Global Canopy Height tiles
task_description: The script downloads ETH Global Canopy Height 10m raster tiles (2020) from a shared cloud link, based on user-defined extent and CRS. It transforms the input extent to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), calculates overlapping 3-degree latitude/longitude tile boundaries, constructs filenames following the pattern 'ETH_GlobalCanopyHeight_10m_2020_NxxExxx_Map.tif' (or S/W variants), checks for local existence, and downloads missing tiles to a designated directory. Outputs include download success status per tile and logging of progress or errors.

The script imports and restructures PRISMA Level 2C hyperspectral data from HDF5 (.he5) files into a georeferenced, spectrally calibrated GeoTIFF (or VRT) with correct interleave (VNIR + SWIR stacked), geolocation-derived extent and resolution, and embedded spectral metadata (wavelength, FWHM, gain, offset). It reads latitude for spatial extent, extracts VNIR and SWIR cube subdatasets, transposes and stacks them (with VNIR first), creates a raster using _classic.hubdsm with WGS84 projection, and optionally writes spectral metadata and radiometric calibration parameters to the output file. The script does not perform classification, modeling, or time-series analysis — it is a data ingestion and preprocessing utility for PRISMA L2C products. Study area, time range, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code; the spatial extent is dynamically derived from the Latitude subdataset's QGIS layer extent, but no fixed location is hardcoded or implied. Satellite: PRISMA; sensor: Hyperspectral Imaging Spectrometer (HIS); bands: all VNIR (128 bands) and SWIR (288 bands) channels, though exact band indices or names are not extracted or used individually.

The script performs hydraulic infrastructure analysis on a water distribution or pressure sewer system modeled in QGIS using the qepanet plugin. It validates topological connectivity between pipes and junctions/reservoirs, builds connection and incidence matrices, assigns zone IDs based on pipe diameter changes or user-defined end nodes, computes elevation-based attributes (minimum elevation, static head), calculates total dynamic head, and exports results back to QGIS vector layers for visualization. Key methods include spatial indexing with QgsSpatialIndex to find pipe start/end nodes, pandas DataFrame manipulation for attribute aggregation by zone, and matrix operations using numpy to infer upstream/downstream relationships. Outputs include updated 'Pipes' and 'Junctions' vector layers with computed properties (e.g., Zone ID, Diameter [in], Static Head [ft], Total Dynamic Head [ft]), a summary Zone_props table aggregating per-zone metrics (e.g., Max Flow [gpm], Friction Loss Factor [ft/100ft], Min Elevation [ft]), and QGIS feature selection of disconnected elements. The analysis assumes a directed tree graph with exactly one reservoir as the sole outlet; no satellite, remote sensing, or temporal data is used — all inputs are local QGIS vector layers (pipes_vlay, junctions_vlay, reservoirs_vlay, etc.) and user-defined parameters (e.g., pipe material, C-factor, lateral_conn_dia).

task_name: Sample VIIRS night fire locations with raster values
task_description: The script samples raster values (from a single GeoTIFF named 'one.tif') at VIIRS night fire point locations (from 'ssea_2012_N.shp'), filters points where the sampled value is ≥ 1, and exports the selected points as a new shapefile ('onesampled.shp'). The study area is implied by file paths containing 'ssea_2012_N' (likely South/Southeast Asia) and '2012SA' (2012 South Asia), with time context from filename 'ssea_2012_N.shp' indicating 2012. Data sources are local vector (VIIRS night fires) and local raster (unspecified origin, possibly land cover or fire-related raster); no satellite, sensor, or band information is present in the code — all geospatial operations are performed via QGIS's 'rastersampling' algorithm and attribute-based selection. Final output is a filtered shapefile of fire points intersecting raster cells with value ≥ 1.

The script performs arbitrary NumPy-based mathematical operations on user-provided raster and vector layers, supporting band selection (by name, index, or wavelength), mask handling, spatial resampling to a common grid, vector rasterization, block-wise or monolithic processing, and dynamic output raster generation. It does not fix a specific analysis—its purpose is general-purpose raster algebra: inputs are dynamically mapped from QGIS parameters (R1–R10, V1–V10, RS list) or hard-coded layer declarations in code comments; outputs are determined by variable assignments in the user-supplied Python/NumPy expression (e.g., 'out = R1 * R2 + V1Mask'). No fixed study area, time range, sensor, or classification method is embedded—the workflow is entirely data- and code-driven via QGIS Processing interface.

The script computes a vector cutline polygon that represents the largest contiguous area derived from edge-detection and optimal path routing on a single-band orthophoto raster. It reads an orthophoto file (e.g., GeoTIFF), optionally scales it for efficiency, applies Canny edge detection to identify boundaries, constructs vertical and horizontal line probes with padded offsets, assigns high cost ('lava') to probe lines and low cost to edges, computes least-cost paths across the cost surface using Dijkstra-based routing (via skimage.graph.route_through_array), converts resulting pixel paths to geographic LineStrings, simplifies them, unions and polygonizes the linestrings, filters polygons by containment within an optional crop-area geometry (if provided), selects the largest-area polygon, and exports it as a GeoPackage (.gpkg) containing a single Polygon feature. Inputs are local filesystem raster (orthophoto) and optional vector crop boundary; no GEE server-side assets or time-series are used — all operations are client-side (rasterio, scikit-image, shapely, QGIS processing). Study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and bands are not specified — the script is agnostic to acquisition source and operates solely on pre-processed orthophoto data.

The script models and visualizes transportation trip matrices between zones using QGIS PyQGIS. It loads zone, network, and centroid shapefiles; computes trip volumes from TRANUS model outputs (CSV trip matrix files); joins trip data to line geometries representing origin-destination connections; applies graduated symbology (color or size) based on trip volume; and persists configuration and results in SQLite and XML. Key operations include memory layer creation, attribute joins, WKT geometry parsing, QgsGraduatedSymbolRenderer application, and custom project variable management.

The script tests the MetadataEditorDialog class in the EnMAP-Box QGIS plugin, verifying its ability to handle supported data sources (raster layers like ENVI-formatted EnMAP and HiRes imagery, and vector layers like landcover_polygon) within a QGIS project context. It checks dialog instantiation, layer association, EnMAPBox integration, and GUI responsiveness. No geospatial analysis, classification, or export of derived products occurs; the outputs are test assertions and interactive GUI displays for developer validation.

The script is a QGIS unit test suite that verifies the correctness of the QgsProviderSublayerDetails class implementation — including getter/setter methods, equality comparison, layer conversion (toLayer), and MIME URI generation. It uses synthetic and local test data (e.g., 'lines.shp' from unitTestDataPath()) to validate behavior. No geospatial analysis, modeling, or remote sensing operations are performed; it is purely software testing code for QGIS provider registry internals. All assertions confirm expected state transitions and object equivalence under controlled conditions.

task_name: Map flood extent using SAR and optical water indices
task_description: The script loads and visualizes multi-source flood-related raster layers for a specific month (e.g., '03/2025') in QGIS. It constructs a layered visualization stack (bottom to top): Sentinel-2 true color (B2/B3/B4), S2 NDWI, S3 NDWI (if enabled), Dynamic World water probability, and SAR-derived water mask or flood difference layer. The SAR input is resolved dynamically from multiple glob patterns targeting water masks or flood-difference rasters derived from Sentinel-1 (S1) data. Styling uses custom pseudo-color ramps with transparency: SAR water masks use cyan-to-dark-blue ramp; SAR flood-difference uses diverging red–white–blue ramp; NDWI layers use blue-to-dark-blue ramps; DW water probability uses sequential blue ramp. True color styling applies contrast enhancement (min=300, max=3500) to scaled Sentinel-2 surface reflectance bands. All layers are grouped under 'Flood 3-layer YYYY-MM' and optionally zoomed to extent. Study area is implied by file paths (e.g., 'flood_30km', 'water_evolution_10km_2025'), suggesting a regional flood monitoring context — but no explicit geographic boundary or geometry is defined in code. Data sources include precomputed local GeoTIFFs (not GEE assets), so no Earth Engine server-side processing occurs; this is a QGIS automation script for loading and styling locally stored flood products.

The script calculates spatially explicit delivered cost of timber harvesting by integrating road network data, terrain (slope and elevation), hydrologic barriers (streams and waterbodies), and operational constraints. It uses OpenStreetMap (OSM) for roads and hydrography, and 3DEP (or fallback SRTM) DEM for elevation. Key steps include: (1) snapping sawmill points to nearest road segments; (2) computing on-road hauling cost using speed-based conversion factors; (3) performing cost-distance analysis from roads across terrain and barriers to estimate off-road extraction distance and time; (4) applying slope-dependent felling costs (e.g., $15/ton for slope ≤35%, $27/ton otherwise); (5) adding processing ($56/ton), hand treatment ($2470/ha), and prescribed fire ($2470/ha) costs; (6) assigning skidder vs. cable harvesting systems based on slope and road proximity thresholds (≤35% + within 460 m of road → skidder; else cable). Outputs are raster files: 'Delivered Cost' (USD/ton), 'Additional Treatment Cost' (USD/ha), and optional rasters including 'Skidder Cost', 'Cable Cost', 'Potential Harvesting System', and treatment-specific costs. All processing occurs in EPSG:5070 (NAD83 Conus Albers).

The script models passive margin wedge (PMW) geometry and sediment thickness along profiles derived from multi-point features representing passive margins. It computes crest positions (X_CREST, Z_CREST), raster-sampled bathymetry (Z_RASTER), wedge extent (X_MAX), and integrates abyssal sediment thickness and density to derive node-level properties (Z_WITH_SED, H_SED, RHO_SED) for each point along PMW profiles. Inputs include age-dependent parametric passive margin models (PMConversionTools), raster-derived depth (qgis_tin_raster_prelim_*.tif), continent polygon boundaries, and sediment property functions (SEDConversionTools). Outputs are GeoJSON files: PMW_profiles_*.geojson (multi-point profile geometries) and PMW_nodes_*.geojson (point features with geophysical attributes per age slice).

The script shifts the georeferenced bounding box of an input raster by user-specified X and Y offsets (in CRS units) using GDAL Translate with outputBounds. It reads the input raster’s extent via QGIS layer extent, applies the shift to all four corner coordinates (ulx, uly, lrx, lry), and writes a new raster file with updated geotransform and extent. No resampling, reprojection, or pixel value modification occurs — only coordinate system alignment adjustment. Input is any GDAL-readable raster loaded in QGIS; output is a shifted GeoTIFF (or other format per destination path). Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification, or analysis methods are not involved — this is a pure georeferencing correction utility.

The script performs a spatial point-in-polygon query against a FlatGeobuf (FGB) file containing metadata and geometry footprints of aerial imagery sheets over New Zealand. It uses NZTM2000 (EPSG:2193) coordinates, applies a padded bounding box filter leveraging the FGB’s Hilbert R-tree index for efficient HTTP Range requests via GDAL /vsicurl/, then tests exact point containment using OGR geometry operations. Outputs are dictionaries of feature properties (e.g., 'asset_id', 'year', '_wkt') sorted newest-first by extracted 4-digit year; no classification, modeling, or spectral analysis is performed — only spatial indexing and attribute retrieval. Study area is New Zealand (inferred from EPSG:2193 and domain 'imagery.mutant.kiwi'); time range is not specified in the script; data source is a single static FGB file hosted at https://imagery.mutant.kiwi/all_imagery.fgb; no satellite, sensor, or bands are involved — this is vector metadata, not raster imagery processing.

The script imports geophysical data from an HDF5 file and converts it either into a QGIS vector point layer (using latitude/longitude/value arrays) or a raster layer via GDAL rasterization. It reads user-selected datasets (e.g., 'latitude', 'longitude', and a main data variable like 'temperature' or 'precipitation') from arbitrary HDF5 files, filters out NaN and _FillValue entries, and constructs geometry accordingly. No fixed study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is embedded in the code — all inputs are user-selected at runtime via GUI. Outputs are ephemeral QGIS layers: either a memory-based point vector layer with attribute 'value', or a GeoTIFF raster generated from those points using gdal.Rasterize with user-defined pixel size and NoData value. The script does not perform analysis, modeling, classification, or temporal aggregation — only format conversion and spatial representation.

The script imports a Landsat Level 2 (surface reflectance) product from its MTL.txt metadata file, constructs a VRT (Virtual Raster) containing all surface reflectance bands, applies radiometric scaling (gain/offset) per collection standard, assigns ENVI-compliant wavelength metadata and band descriptions, and outputs a georeferenced, spectrally annotated raster layer with values scaled to 0–1. It supports Landsat 4–9 (LT, LE, LC, LO prefixes), Collection 1 and 2, and explicitly handles band numbering, naming, and central wavelengths per sensor (e.g., OLI/TIRS for LC/LO, ETM+ for LE, TM for LT). No classification, time-series analysis, or spatial subsetting is performed — only format conversion, metadata injection, and radiometric normalization. Study area, time range, and location are not specified in the code; inputs are file-path driven and agnostic to geography or date.

The script tests GDAL-based geospatial raster processing algorithms, specifically validating command-line generation for operations including hillshade, slope, aspect, color relief, contouring, raster clipping (by extent/mask), reprojection (warp), resampling, gridding, and raster-vector conversions. It uses synthetic test data (e.g., 'dem.tif', 'points.gml') located in a local 'testdata' directory — no real-world study area, time range, or satellite data is involved. All tests are unit tests verifying correct GDAL CLI argument construction (e.g., 'gdaldem hillshade', 'gdalwarp', 'gdal_translate'), not actual Earth Engine (GEE) execution. The outputs are asserted command strings, not geospatial products.

The script performs regression-based unmixing to estimate sub-pixel class fractions (e.g., endmember abundances) from a raster layer using synthetically mixed training data derived from a classification dataset of spectral endmembers. It trains an ensemble of regressors (one per run) on synthetically generated mixtures—controlled by mixing probabilities, within-class allowance, background proportion, and class sampling weights—then predicts fraction maps per class, aggregates predictions across the ensemble (using mean±std or median±IQR), stacks results into a multi-band fraction raster with band names and colors matching input categories, optionally generates a hard classification map via probability-to-class conversion, and outputs a variation raster quantifying prediction uncertainty. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or sensor bands are referenced in the code—the input raster and classification dataset are generic file-based inputs (e.g., .pkl endmember library, arbitrary GeoTIFF), and all operations are algorithmic (synthetic mixing, scikit-learn regression, GDAL-based stacking/aggregation), not Earth Engine image collection processing.

The script evaluates the performance of a susceptibility model (e.g., landslide, hazard, or risk) using ROC curves, QQ plots, and statistical metrics (AUC, F1, Cohen's Kappa, MAE, RMSE, R², Pearson correlation). It loads geospatial input data from a GeoPackage, extracts predictor variables and a target variable ('y'), computes prediction scores ('SI'), and generates diagnostic visualizations (ROC, cross-validated ROC, QQ plots for training and CV folds) and saves results back to a GeoPackage with geometry and attributes. The workflow is driven by user-defined parameters including input vector layer, variable names, target field ('lsd'), family ('gaussian', 'MLP_regressor', etc.), scaling options, and output directory.

The script extracts shorelines from Sentinel-1 SAR imagery using water mask classification and vector boundary processing. It downloads pre-processed SAR water masks (binary) and RGB composites (VV, VH, VV-VH) over user-defined AOI and date range via Google Earth Engine; tiles the AOI into 0.05° grids for scalable download; merges downloaded GeoTIFF tiles; resamples and georeferences the water mask; converts raster water mask to vector polygons; simplifies and buffers boundaries to derive smooth shoreline linestrings; outputs a GeoJSON file of shoreline features (LinearRing geometries) in EPSG:3857; and adds both the merged SAR RGB raster and shoreline vector layer to the QGIS project. Input AOI is selected from loaded QGIS vector layers; no explicit study area name or coordinates are hardcoded — location is fully user-driven via QGIS interface. Satellite data source is Sentinel-1 (C-band SAR), processed via custom `waterMask_download` function (imported from `.Plugin_download`).

The script is a QGIS plugin GUI for batch importing GPX files (GPS Exchange Format) into QGIS as vector layers. It supports importing waypoints, tracks, and routes from user-specified folders; allows selection of geometry type (point/line/polygon), CRS (default EPSG:4326), field inclusion/exclusion (e.g., 'name', 'time', 'ele'), extent-based spatial filtering (using current map canvas extent), subfolder scanning, and error handling (valid/invalid GPX output folders). Outputs are QGIS vector layers with user-defined naming, projection, and attribute schema — no raster, satellite, or Earth Engine (GEE) processing occurs. The script does not perform classification, modeling, time-series analysis, or remote sensing operations; it is purely a desktop GIS data ingestion tool. All logic operates locally via QGIS Python API and PyQt5 — no Google Earth Engine code is present in the provided script.

This script is a QGIS Processing test suite for GDAL raster algorithms, not an Earth Engine (GEE) script. It validates the correct generation of GDAL command-line invocations for geospatial raster operations—including projection assignment, translation, clipping, contouring, gridding, hillshading, slope/aspect calculation, color relief, proximity analysis, rasterization, warping, merging, and more—using synthetic test data (e.g., 'dem.tif', 'points.gml', 'polys.gml'). It does not process real-world Earth observation data, define a study area, apply time filters, or export final geospatial products; rather, it verifies algorithm parameter-to-command mapping via unit tests. All inputs are local test files under 'testdata/', with no remote satellite data, time series, or geographic extent specified beyond generic CRS codes (e.g., EPSG:3111, EPSG:4326).
